summary: Colonial stone tower built with Philadelphia lottery money; replaced by an automatic light in 1924 and undermined by the sea, it fell from its dune on 13 April 1926.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Sources give 1764 (USLHS; Lighthouse Service 1937 review: 'built by the Colony in 1764'), 1765 (Putnam: cost of the work included 'expense of oil from the year 1765'; Lighthouse Service 1926: built 1765 to 1767), about 1767 (Putnam, completion) and 1769 (Wikipedia; Lewes archive citing Coast Guard records). The record's two first_lit events (1764, 1769) are thus different readings of the same light; 1765 is the earliest date a source ties to oil being burned. Left for a human to settle.

Wikidata's 1926 end date is the collapse of the abandoned tower on 13 April 1926. The light itself was discontinued on 1 October 1924, replaced by an automatic light on a skeleton tower (last shone 30 September 1924 according to the Milford Chronicle).

Tower height is 69 ft 3 in (21 m) in the Lewes archive and Wikipedia (which the record follows), 82 ft from base to centre of lantern in the 1908 Light List entry kept by USLHS, and about 93 ft in LighthouseFriends. Focal height 164 ft (50 m) above water is the Light List figure.

notes_for_editor: 1) First-lit date is disputed (1764/1765/1767/1769); see resolved_conflicts. 2) The record's characteristic 'Fl W with R sector' is not supported by any source read: LighthouseFriends calls it a fixed light in 1817, and the 1924 replacement light was 'fixed white, acetylene' (Bulletin 1924, which misprints the state as N.J.). The characteristic was left out of facts.light. 3) Record location (38.7772, -75.0786, LighthouseFriends) is about 0.6 km from the 1908 Light List position kept by USLHS (38 46.42 N, 75 05.03 W = 38.7737, -75.0838) and from Wikipedia's 38.7783, -75.0845; the site is now offshore so no correction is proposed. 4) Cause of the 1777 fire is told three ways (Putnam: partly burned; LighthouseFriends: British after an encounter with the keeper; Secrets of the Eastern Shore: probably legend); the Lighthouse Service's 1937 review instead puts the burned interior steps in the War of 1812, and its year of rebuilding is garbled in the scan ('18,10'). 5) The Lighthouse Board reports for 1850-1890 are not in the local corpus and were not read; the 19th century rests on Putnam, USLHS and LighthouseFriends. Lens date 1855 (LF) vs 1856 (USLHS) is unresolved. 6) LighthouseFriends is a modern copyrighted site and was used for facts only, in our own words. The 1924-1926 newspaper quotations come through Secrets of the Eastern Shore except the Milford Chronicle of 16 April 1926, which was read at Chronicling America; the Wilmington papers cited there (Evening Journal, News Journal) were not read directly. 7) The USLHS roster and LighthouseFriends differ in small ways: Palmer head keeper 1919 (USLHS) vs 1920 (LF); LF adds Joseph M. Daisey (second assistant 1920) and Charles C. West (1920), which USLHS does not list; spellings Hasting/Hastings and Williams/William follow the USLHS roster, with the variants noted on the lines. The 1918-23 Bulletin index prints 'Gray, John T.'; the Bulletin text prints John C. Gr[a]y. 8) Dagworthy D. Joseph's obituary (as transcribed by USLHS) says 'more than thirty years' while the register span is 1869-1910 (41 years) and the Rehoboth Beach museum says 40; John Joseph (1865-69) and Henry D. Joseph (1869-73) were assistants, and the obituary names his father as Henry D. Joseph, but no source read says they are the same people, so no relationship is stated. USLHS also lists two contractors (James Hall, Joseph Lyndall) without dates; they are not in the roster. 9) Bulletin 1923 prints the day of the mule-team rescue as 'March 2(?)' (damaged OCR) between entries for 21 and 26 March; LighthouseFriends says 26 March. The story says 'March 1923'. 10a) The council minutes of 12 Nov 1778 are badly OCR'd: the sum reads 'Forty-Biz Pounds twelre Shillings A six Pence' and is read here as 46 pounds 12 shillings 6 pence; the words 'Light House' are inferred from 'attending the ^A^ Honse' and 'the ligK Hom'. A page image check is advisable. 10) The replica in Rehoboth Beach is dated 1924 (moved 2004) by Wikipedia and the Lewes archive but 2004 by LighthouseFriends. 11) The Milford Chronicle (16 Apr 1926) says a northeast gale and unusually high tide; the Lewes archive (after John W. Beach) says a clear day and a northeast breeze. Both are reported. The Chronicle also has errors (built by the British in 1765; De Braak in 1789), so it is used only for the fall. 12) Fact-check 2026-10-21: the Wilmington Evening Journal (July 1924, 1925) and Wilmington News Journal (14 April 1926) passages are cited to the Secrets of the Eastern Shore article and are described in the story as second-hand. 'Captain Gray' is not identified by first name in that article. LighthouseFriends calls Everett C. Johnson the commission's secretary; the blog says he headed it. 13) Putnam is no longer called 'the historian' (the cited pages do not give his office). 14) The council-minute sum (46 pounds 12s 6d) rests on a single OCR copy; a page-image check remains advisable. 15) The Light-House Board items dated 1895, 1897 and 1899 are from reports for the fiscal years ended 30 June of those years.
